correctness.rationale: For girth at least six, every pair at distance two has a unique midpoint. Every face inside a closed graph-neighborhood simplex but outside G can be paired with its unique center, in descending face-size order, giving a complete elementary collapse B to G. A triangle outside B consists of three distance-two pairs and their distinct midpoints, so yields a simple six-cycle; each six-cycle yields exactly its two alternating triangles. Any fourth vertex within distance two of such a triple would force a second hexagon sharing edges with the first (or a 3-, 4-, or 5-cycle), hence is excluded by the all-hexagons edge-disjoint hypothesis. Thus K is obtained from B by two 2-cell attachments along each six-cycle loop. After B collapses, delete one private graph edge together with the first 2-cell for each hexagon; the second cell becomes a free \(S^2\) summand. This proves for arbitrary graph order that K is a wedge of b-h circles and h spheres, with the claimed integral homology map. The standalone checker independently verifies the local classification, actual free-face steps and complete GF2 Betti numbers on nine finite examples. A computation alone would not establish the universal theorem.

Both differ from the present positive-hexagon all-graph formula. Full primary text of Adamaszek et al., arXiv:1712.06224, Theorem 3.15 and Proposition 4.1 covers certain short-path metric gluings; overlapping cases, such as bouquets of cycles, are credited, but the theta(3,3,4) member cannot arise via those one-point/one-edge circle attachments, and a common path of length three violates their strict alpha<ell/3 bound. The full arXiv:2302.14388 primarily classifies Platonic-solid vertex sets, not arbitrary high-girth graphs with edge-disjoint hexagons. Searches for six-cycle packing, square-graph clique-complex attachments and mixed \(S^1\)/\(S^2\) wedges found no exact or dominating primary formulation. This is a literature-based noncoverage comparison, not a proof of global originality.

value.rationale: The first sharp failure of graph-power homotopy stability occurs at girth six: every isolated six-cycle creates a two-dimensional class while simultaneously killing an integral graph-cycle class. The edge-disjointness hypothesis is a natural noninteraction condition and gives the complete mixed-dimensional homotopy type and exact persistent transition on an infinite class of branching, vertex-sharing and noncactus graphs. The result is stronger than Betti counts and does not merely rename the known single-\(C_6\) example or the girth-seven collapse. No new statement about higher scales or arbitrary overlapping hexagons is asserted.
